projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Joseph Russo was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: ...born [birth date redacted] to an Italian father and an English-Irish-Scottish mother. In 1940, having turned 18 years old, I joined the Army at Fort Winfield Scott, San Francisco.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: Where did you grow up?

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: In the East Bay, San Francisco-Oakland, called San Francisco-Oakland, East Bay area.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: Okay. And then?

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: On July 1st, 1940, I joined the Army in Fort Winfield Scott, San Francisco having just become 18 years old. I was assigned to Headquarters Battery and Sixth Coast Artillery which was the hardware entrance control battery of San Francisco Bay. We were responsible for the line lane and the nets which closed off the Golden Gate entrance to San Francisco Bay. When the War began, I was at home for the weekend, returned to Fort Winfield Scott and went on 25th Avenue Gate as the sentinel for four to six hours before we were relieved. Later, we fortified the what is now called, or what was then called, BakerÂ’s Beach when the machine guns and barbed wire in order to stop any Japanese invasion that may come to San Francisco. The harbor entrance control post was turned over to neo-operations in 1941, Â’42. I had applied for West Point and took the regular army entrance examination of which I ended up 29 out of 50 on the Army list. Congress increased the first 25 entered the Academy on time. Congress increased the quota on who entered on the second 25 in July of 1942. I took pilot training at Guider Field on Park, Arkansas in 1944. Although we finished primary, we did not go on to basic training 18-13 or 18-6 at Stewart Field, New York since they didnÂ’t need any more pilots at that particular time. I graduated in Â’45 and went to the Philippine Islands as a Second Lieutenant. There were Japanese that didnÂ’t know the war was over when we arrived in the Philippines. Therefore, there was some fighting. Later, I fought the red insurgents which are the Hukbalahaps at that particular time.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: What type installation - what duties did you have when you first went to the Philippines?

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: I was an executive officer for more than one battery, or I was the only officer in a battery besides the battery commander.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: And that was for - what kind of battery was it?

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: As an anti-aircraft battery, gun battery.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: What was the name of it?

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: 90-millimeter.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: The name of the field there was -

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: San Marcelino.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: San Marcelino.

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: Later, I flew the father of the O-19 which is an L-9 or 10 down in Manila because of the - the regular pilots were tired of making the, as we call, the milk run, up to San Marcelino at that time. Part of the flight was over Baton Pass and Manila Bay. We landed at the Wack Wack (W-A-C) Country Club landing strip in Manila. I attended the University of Virginia in 1948 to Â’50 to get my Masters in Nuclear Physics. Later returned to Fort Bliss -- became a radar instructor.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: Well, when you finished your duty there at the Philippines in San Marcelino Field, what did you do next after that?

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: I was - I became a battery commander of -- while I was -- I had several jobs. I was a range officer and fired units going to Okinawa, 90-millimeter batteries. They were eventually stationed in Okinawa to protect against Japanese raids.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: Okay. Then after that, after Okinawa, where did you go?

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: Went to Japan and back to Fort Bliss where I was in a composite battery of 90s, 40s, 50s, quad 50s. Later, I was a test officer for 120s on Oro Grande for and against two targets flown above 30,000 feet. We were firing 120-millimeter anti-aircraft gun that the Army had developed. I would have to shut down firing in Oro Grande since they were firing V-2Â’s from White Sands missile range.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: Okay. Then was it after that or before that that you went to -

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: I went after that. I went in 1948 to Â’50. I went to University of Virginia - get my Masters in Nuclear Physics. Returning to Fort Bliss in 1950, they needed a radar instructorÂ’s -- radar maintenance -- maintenance radar instructors, of which I became one -- later taught SCR 784, kilometer radar mechanics or maintenance men of which they were being killed in Korea faster than we could put them out of that school. After finishing the advanced course and a tour in the Pentagon, I returned to Fort Bliss and became an Army Hawk Battalion commander -- Sixth Battalion, 56 Artillery. It was a strike battalion. I later took the initial Army Hawk Battalion to Vietnam in 1966, and after being relieved of my battalion after three years, I went to Magpie Headquarters and Special Ops -- 3T22 section of Magpie Headquarters -- and was the artillery officer for Magpie under General LeFeu who was the 3 -- J3 at that time.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: Then - and then where?

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: Then taught at Howards, retired from the Army in 1975 as a colonel, director of Combat Developments.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: Where was that location when you retired?

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: Fort Bliss.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: And what was your - what was your career after the military? Now you had -- that was 35 years.

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: Yeah, 35 years. And then taught at UTEP, University of Texas, El Paso, UTEP - for close to seven years as instruction to computers using FORTRAN language and then worked for three civilian organizations who supported the combat developments RAM, COLSA, and MPRI for the next close to 15, 15 years retiring completely in 1993. I volunteered my time to the police station, El Paso Police Department, and a War Eagle Air Museum of the last ten years.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: What was one of the early and main projects you worked on at the War Eagles Museum?

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: Airplane-wise was the MiG 21 which builds - and I put the wings on the MiG 21 when it came in from Germany. I also worked on the Russian plane that is outside the office over there.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: The Tupolev?

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: Yeah, Tupolev, Tu-2. Tu-2.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: I should have asked this way back at the beginning, but when you were talking about the coastal artillery, about what was the size and range of those guns?

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: The first, the range of the 90s, I later manned the first anti-aircraft gun I was the 37-millimeter with 250s on the side, about a half-track vehicle. Later joined a 90-millimeter anti-aircraft battery which firing range was less than 20,000 feet altitude at that particular time, and -

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: About what year did radar come into being in terms of being able to help direct anti-aircraft fire?

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: IÂ’m not sure, but we had the SER-584s in 1940 - Â’47, I guess.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: Were the Germans using radar directed anti-aircraft fire before we got it?

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: No, the Germans were not.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: I know they had some late in the War, but I wasnÂ’t sure if they had it first or if we did.

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: The British had it first.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: The British did.

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: Which is confirmed by some other people.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: Joe, on behalf of the War Eagles Air Museum, I want to thank you for sharing your experience with us and really appreciate your time and effort.

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: If you want to see a picture, thereÂ’s a glamour picture in the office made in 1944 with a helmet and goggles that we wore at that time during pilot training.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: Where is that located?

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: ItÂ’s in the office out there at the desk where you sign in.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: Yes. Was it pictures of what you actually wore or just of that time?

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: At that time. It was all the students going through pilot training of which Jack Bell also has a glamour picture located in the museum with goggles and helmet, and they called them "glamour pictures" 'cause all the girls wanted pictures of aviators.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: [Laughter]. I think thatÂ’s still true somewhat, but the helmets now are a lot different than they were then.

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: ThatÂ’s right.

sp.speaker: William Messersmith
sp.p: Okay. As we finish this, weÂ’ll take a look.

sp.speaker: Joseph Russo
sp.p: Yeah. ItÂ’s at the-- [End of recording]
